questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the most suitable method for the preparation of allylphenylether?
questions.solution:
The preparation of allyl phenyl ether involves the Williamson ether synthesis, which is a nucleophilic substitution reaction between an alkoxide or phenoxide ion and an alkyl halide.

The reaction requires a phenoxide ion (nucleophile) and an allyl halide (electrophile).

Option (2) shows the reaction between sodium phenoxide ($C_{6}H_{5}ONa$) and allyl bromide ($CH_{2}=CH-CH_{2}Br$). This is a classic $S_{N}2$ reaction where the phenoxide oxygen attacks the primary allylic carbon, displacing the bromide ion to form allyl phenyl ether ($C_{6}H_{5}-O-CH_{2}-CH=CH_{2}$).

Option (1) involves vinyl bromide, which is unreactive towards $S_{N}2$ substitution due to the partial double bond character of the $C-Br$ bond and the instability of the vinyl cation. Option (3) involves a vinyl halide and methoxide. Option (4) involves benzyl bromide and an allyl alkoxide, which would produce allyl benzyl ether, not allyl phenyl ether.

Answer:

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their acidic strength 4-chlorophenol (I), 4-methylphenol(II), 4-nitrophenol(III), 4-methoxyphenol(IV) and phenol(V)
questions.solution:
The acidic strength of substituted phenols depends on the electronic effects of the substituents attached to the benzene ring. Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) increase acidity by stabilizing the phenoxide ion through inductive (-I) or resonance (-M) effects, while electron-donating groups (EDG) decrease acidity by destabilizing the phenoxide ion through inductive (+I) or resonance (+M) effects.

The substituents in the given compounds are:
I: 4-chlorophenol (Cl group, -I effect, +M effect; overall -I effect dominates, making it more acidic than phenol).
II: 4-methylphenol (C$H_{3}$ group, +I effect and hyperconjugation, making it less acidic than phenol). \\ III: 4-nitrophenol (NO_{2}$ group, strong -I and -M effects, making it the most acidic).
IV: 4-methoxyphenol (OCH_{3}$ group, +M effect dominates over -I effect, making it the least acidic). \\ V: Phenol (reference compound). \\ \\ Comparing the effects: \\ The -M effect of NO_{2}$ in III is very strong, making it the most acidic. The -I effect of Cl in I makes it more acidic than phenol. The +I and hyperconjugation of CH_{3}$ in II make it less acidic than phenol. The +M effect of OCH_{3}$ in IV is stronger than the +I effect of CH_{3}$, making IV the least acidic. \\ \\ The order of increasing acidic strength is: IV < II < V < I < III. \\ \\ Answer: IV $ \lt $ II $ \lt $ V $ \lt $ I $ \lt $ III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following compounds will not give Iodoform reaction?
questions.solution:
The iodoform test is given by compounds containing the $CH_{3}CO-$ group or the $CH_{3}CH(OH)-$ group.

Ethanol is $CH_{3}CH_{2}OH$, which contains the $CH_{3}CH(OH)-$ group. It gives a positive iodoform test.

Isobutyl alcohol is $(CH_{3})_{2}CHCH_{2}OH$. This structure does not contain the $CH_{3}CH(OH)-$ group. Therefore, it does not give the iodoform reaction.

3-methyl-2-butanone is $CH_{3}COCH(CH_{3})_{2}$, which contains the $CH_{3}CO-$ group. It gives a positive iodoform test.

Propan-2-ol is $CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3}$, which contains the $CH_{3}CH(OH)-$ group. It gives a positive iodoform test.

Answer: Isobutyl alcohol

In which one of the case the chemical reaction given in Column I does not match with the name of the reaction given in Column II?
$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \text{S.No.} & \text{Column I - Reactions} & \text{Column II - Name of reaction.} \\ \hline \text{A} & \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{CHO}+ \text{Conc. NaOH, heat} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{OH}+\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{COONa} & \text{Cannizzaro's reaction} \\ \hline \text{B} & \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{CH}_3+ \text{ (i) } \mathrm{CrO}_2 \mathrm{Cl}_2 / \mathrm{CS}_2 \text{ (ii) } \mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{O}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{CHO} & \text{Etard reaction.} \\ \hline \text{C} & \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_6+\mathrm{CO} / \mathrm{HCl} \text{ (anh. } \mathrm{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{CHO} & \text{Kolbe's reaction} \\ \hline \text{D} & \mathrm{RCN}+ \text{ (i) } \mathrm{SnCl}_2+\mathrm{HCl} \text{ (ii) } \rightarrow \mathrm{RCHO} & \text{Stephen's reaction.} \\ \hline \end{array}$
questions.solution:
Reaction A is the Cannizzaro reaction, which involves the self-oxidation and reduction of an aldehyde lacking $\alpha$-hydrogens in the presence of a concentrated base. This is correctly matched.

Reaction B is the Etard reaction, which uses chromyl chloride ($\mathrm{CrO}_2 \mathrm{Cl}_2$) to oxidize toluene to benzaldehyde. This is correctly matched.

Reaction C is the Gattermann-Koch reaction, which involves the formylation of benzene using $\mathrm{CO}$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$ in the presence of anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl}_3$ to produce benzaldehyde. The name given in the table is Kolbe's reaction, which is incorrect. Kolbe's reaction refers to the carboxylation of phenol to salicylic acid using $\mathrm{CO}_2$ and $\mathrm{NaOH}$.

Reaction D is the Stephen reduction, which uses $\mathrm{SnCl}_2$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$ to reduce nitriles to imines, which are then hydrolyzed to aldehydes. This is correctly matched.

Answer: C

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Aldol condensation reaction between which of the following pair of compounds followed by dehydration gives 3-phenylprop-2-en-1-al?
questions.solution:
The target product is 3-phenylprop-2-en-1-al, which has the structure $C_{6}H_{5}-CH=CH-CHO$.

This compound is an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated aldehyde. Aldol condensation between an aldehyde containing an $\alpha$-hydrogen and another carbonyl compound followed by dehydration typically yields such products.

The structure $C_{6}H_{5}-CH=CH-CHO$ can be retrosynthetically broken down at the double bond into benzaldehyde ($C_{6}H_{5}CHO$) and acetaldehyde ($CH_{3}CHO$).

The reaction proceeds as follows: Benzaldehyde ($C_{6}H_{5}CHO$) reacts with acetaldehyde ($CH_{3}CHO$) in the presence of a dilute base. Acetaldehyde provides the $\alpha$-hydrogen to form an enolate, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde to form 3-hydroxy-3-phenylpropanal. Subsequent dehydration of this aldol product yields 3-phenylprop-2-en-1-al (cinnamaldehyde).

Answer: Benzaldehyde and Acetaldehyde

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their reactivity in nucleophilic addition reactions. p-nitrobenzaldehyde (I); methylphenylketone (II); benzaldehyde (III); 4-methylbenzaldehyde (IV)
questions.solution:
The reactivity of carbonyl compounds towards nucleophilic addition reactions is governed by two factors: steric hindrance and electronic effects. Steric hindrance decreases reactivity, while electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) increase reactivity by increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon, and electron-donating groups (EDG) decrease reactivity.

The compounds are: (I) p-nitrobenzaldehyde, (II) methylphenylketone (acetophenone), (III) benzaldehyde, (IV) 4-methylbenzaldehyde.

Comparing the aldehydes (I, III, IV): p-nitrobenzaldehyde (I) has a strong EWG ($-NO_2$), making the carbonyl carbon highly electrophilic. Benzaldehyde (III) has no substituent. 4-methylbenzaldehyde (IV) has a methyl group, which is an EDG (+I and hyperconjugation), reducing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon. Thus, the order for aldehydes is IV < III < I.

Comparing ketones and aldehydes: Methylphenylketone (II) is a ketone, which is less reactive than aldehydes due to both steric hindrance and the +I effect of the methyl group. Therefore, II is the least reactive among the given compounds.

Combining these, the increasing order of reactivity is II < IV < III < I.

Answer: II $ \lt $ IV $ \lt $ III $ \lt $ I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the following compounds
ethanamine (i); diethylamine (ii); aniline (iii) and $N$ - methylbenzenamine (iv) The correct decreasing order of pKb values of the compounds is:
questions.solution:
The basicity of amines is inversely proportional to their $pK_b$ values. Higher basicity corresponds to a lower $pK_b$ value.

Comparing the basicity of the given compounds:
1. Diethylamine (ii) is a secondary aliphatic amine. It is the most basic due to the electron-donating inductive effect of two ethyl groups and favorable solvation.
2. Ethanamine (i) is a primary aliphatic amine. It is less basic than diethylamine due to fewer electron-donating groups.
3. $N$-methylbenzenamine (iv) is an aromatic amine where the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalized into the benzene ring, reducing its availability for protonation. However, the methyl group provides a slight electron-donating effect compared to aniline.
4. Aniline (iii) is a primary aromatic amine where the lone pair is delocalized into the benzene ring. It is the least basic among the given compounds.

The order of basicity is: (ii) > (i) > (iv) > (iii).

Since $pK_b$ is inversely proportional to basicity, the decreasing order of $pK_b$ values is: (iii) > (iv) > (i) > (ii).

Answer: iii $ \gt $ iv $ \gt $ i $ \gt $ ii

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following amines cannot be prepared by Gabriel's phthalimide synthesis?
questions.solution:
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis involves the reaction of potassium phthalimide with an alkyl halide to form an N-alkyl phthalimide, which is subsequently hydrolyzed to yield a primary amine.

The reaction proceeds via an $S_N2$ mechanism. Therefore, the alkyl halide used must be a primary or secondary alkyl halide. Tertiary alkyl halides undergo elimination reactions instead of substitution, and aryl halides do not undergo $S_N2$ reactions with the phthalimide anion.

Analyzing the options:
1. 2-phenylethylamine is a primary amine and can be prepared from 2-phenylethyl chloride.
2. n-propylamine is a primary amine and can be prepared from n-propyl chloride.
3. N-methylbenzylamine is a secondary amine. Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is specifically used for the preparation of primary amines only. It cannot be used to prepare secondary or tertiary amines because the phthalimide anion is a bulky nucleophile and the resulting N-alkyl phthalimide does not allow for further alkylation to form secondary amines.
4. Isobutyl amine is a primary amine and can be prepared from isobutyl chloride.

Thus, N-methylbenzylamine cannot be prepared by this method.

Answer: N-methylbenzylamine

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The major product ' $D$ ' of the following reaction is:
questions.solution:
The starting material is nitrobenzene. Nitrobenzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with $Cl_{2}/AlCl_{3}$. Since the $-NO_{2}$ group is meta-directing, the chlorine atom enters the meta position, forming A, which is 1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene.

In the next step, A (1-chloro-3-nitrobenzene) is treated with $Zn/HCl$, which is a reducing agent. This reduces the nitro group ($-NO_{2}$) to an amino group ($-NH_{2}$), resulting in B, which is 3-chloroaniline.

Next, B (3-chloroaniline) is treated with $HNO_{2}$ at $0-5^{\circ}C$. This is a diazotization reaction, which converts the amino group into a diazonium salt, forming C, which is 3-chlorobenzenediazonium chloride.

Finally, C (3-chlorobenzenediazonium chloride) is treated with $Cu_{2}Br_{2}$ (or $CuBr/HBr$), which is a Sandmeyer reaction. This replaces the diazonium group ($-N_{2}^{+}Cl^{-}$) with a bromine atom, resulting in D, which is 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene.

Answer: 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A polysaccharide $[\mathrm{X}]$ represented as $\left(\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_{10} \mathrm{O}_5\right)$ n serves as a reserve carbohydrate in human beings. An enzyme Phosphorylase breaks it down to glucose when required. It is also found in yeast and fungi. What is $[\mathrm{X}]$ ?
questions.solution:
The polysaccharide represented by the formula $(\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_{10} \mathrm{O}_5)_n$ is a polymer of glucose. Among the given options, glycogen is the primary reserve carbohydrate in humans and animals, stored mainly in the liver and muscles. It is also known as animal starch and is found in yeast and fungi. Glycogen is broken down into glucose-1-phosphate by the enzyme glycogen phosphorylase during glycogenolysis to meet the body's energy requirements. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide in plants, while starch and amylose are reserve carbohydrates in plants.

Answer: Glycogen

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Which of the following statement/s about nucleic acids is/are correct?
i. The chirality of both DNA and RNA molecules is due to the L-sugar component.
ii. The complementary bases in DNA are adenine \& thymine and guanine \& cytosine.
iii. $\quad \beta$-D-glucopyranose is the sugar moiety present in the RNA molecule.
iv. RNA controls the synthesis of proteins.
questions.solution:
Statement (i) is incorrect because the chirality of DNA and RNA is due to the D-sugar component, specifically D-2-deoxyribose in DNA and D-ribose in RNA.

Statement (ii) is correct. In DNA, adenine (A) pairs with thymine (T) via two hydrogen bonds, and guanine (G) pairs with cytosine (C) via three hydrogen bonds.

Statement (iii) is incorrect. The sugar moiety in RNA is $\beta$-D-ribofuranose, not $\beta$-D-glucopyranose.

Statement (iv) is correct. RNA plays a central role in protein synthesis through the processes of transcription and translation.

Since statements (ii) and (iv) are correct, the correct option is (Vj2Fl).

Answer: (ii) and (iv)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which statement is incorrect about aminoacids?
options: $\alpha$-aminoacids are soluble in polar solvents like petroleum ether and benzene.
All aminoacids except glycine are optically active.
At isoelectric point, an aminoacid has the least solubility in water.
questions.solution:
Amino acids are polar compounds due to the presence of both amino and carboxyl groups, which exist as zwitterions in aqueous solutions. Because of their ionic nature, they are highly soluble in water but are insoluble in non-polar organic solvents like petroleum ether and benzene.

Methionine is indeed an essential amino acid, meaning it cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be obtained through diet.

Glycine is the simplest amino acid with the structure $NH_2-CH_2-COOH$. Since the $\alpha$-carbon is attached to two identical hydrogen atoms, it is achiral and thus optically inactive. All other naturally occurring $\alpha$-amino acids possess a chiral $\alpha$-carbon and are optically active.

At the isoelectric point, the net charge on the amino acid is zero. In this state, the electrostatic attractions between the zwitterions are maximized, and the interaction with water molecules is minimized, leading to the lowest solubility in water.

Therefore, the statement that $\alpha$-amino acids are soluble in non-polar solvents like petroleum ether and benzene is incorrect.

Answer: $\alpha$-aminoacids are soluble in polar solvents like petroleum ether and benzene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In which of the following compounds there is a change in hybridisation of the underlined atom.
questions.solution:
In $\underline{\mathrm{Al}} \mathrm{H}_3$, the central Al atom has 3 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs, resulting in $sp^2$ hybridization. In $\underline{\mathrm{Al}} \mathrm{H}_4^{-}$, the Al atom has 4 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs, resulting in $sp^3$ hybridization. Thus, there is a change in hybridization.

In $\mathrm{H}_2 \underline{\mathrm{O}}$, the O atom has 2 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, resulting in $sp^3$ hybridization. In $\mathrm{H}_3 \underline{\mathrm{O}^{+}}$, the O atom has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, resulting in $sp^3$ hybridization. No change occurs.

In $\underline{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{H}_3$, the N atom has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, resulting in $sp^3$ hybridization. In $\underline{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{H}_4^{+}$, the N atom has 4 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs, resulting in $sp^3$ hybridization. No change occurs.

In $\underline{\mathrm{P}} \mathrm{H}_3$, the P atom uses nearly pure p-orbitals for bonding due to Drago's rule, but is often considered $sp^3$ hybridized with a lone pair. In $\underline{\mathrm{P}} \mathrm{H}_4^{+}$, the P atom has 4 bond pairs and 0 lone pairs, resulting in $sp^3$ hybridization. No significant change in hybridization occurs.

Answer: $\underline{\mathrm{Al}} \mathrm{H}_3$ to $\underline{\mathrm{Al}} \mathrm{H}_4^{-}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The chloro compound having the lowest dipole moment is:
questions.solution:
The first image represents (E)-2-chloroprop-1-ene or a similar isomer, but specifically, it is 2-chloroprop-1-ene with a chlorine on each carbon in a trans-like arrangement relative to the double bond. The second image represents 1,1-dichloro-1-propene or a similar isomer. Let us analyze the dipole moments of the given structures.

The first structure shown is (E)-2-chloroprop-1-ene (or trans-1,2-dichloro-1-propene). In this molecule, the two chlorine atoms are on opposite sides of the double bond. The bond dipoles of the C-Cl bonds partially cancel each other out due to their opposite directions, leading to a lower net dipole moment.

The second structure shown is 1,1-dichloro-1-propene. In this molecule, both chlorine atoms are on the same carbon atom. The bond dipoles of the two C-Cl bonds reinforce each other, resulting in a significantly higher net dipole moment.

Comparing the two, the structure in the first image (trans-like arrangement) has a lower net dipole moment than the structure in the second image (geminal arrangement). Among the options provided, the first image corresponds to the isomer with the lower dipole moment.

Answer:

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The pair of molecules that contain odd electron molecule and expanded octet.
questions.solution:
An odd electron molecule is one that contains an unpaired electron in its valence shell. Among the given options, $\mathrm{NO}_2$ has a total of $5 + 6 \times 2 = 17$ valence electrons, which is an odd number, making it an odd electron molecule.

An expanded octet molecule is one where the central atom has more than 8 electrons in its valence shell. In $\mathrm{PCl}_5$, the central phosphorus atom is bonded to five chlorine atoms, resulting in $5 \times 2 = 10$ electrons in its valence shell, which exceeds the octet rule.

Checking other options:
$\mathrm{SF}_6$ has an expanded octet (12 electrons), but $\mathrm{PCl}_5$ also has an expanded octet, not an odd electron molecule.
$\mathrm{BF}_3$ is an electron-deficient molecule (incomplete octet).
$\mathrm{NO}$ is an odd electron molecule, but $\mathrm{AlCl}_3$ is an electron-deficient molecule (incomplete octet).

Therefore, the pair containing an odd electron molecule and an expanded octet is $\mathrm{NO}_2$ and $\mathrm{PCl}_5$.

Answer: $\mathrm{NO}_2, \mathrm{PCl}_5$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For a reaction
$2 A \rightleftharpoons 2 B+C$
2.0 moles of $A$ was placed in a one litre flask and the concentration of $B$ at equilibrium was found to be $0.4 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$. The equilibrium constant at $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is $\qquad\times 10^{-4}$
questions.solution:
The reaction is $2A \rightleftharpoons 2B + C$.

Initial moles: $[A]_0 = 2.0 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$, $[B]_0 = 0$, $[C]_0 = 0$.

At equilibrium, let the concentration of $B$ be $0.4 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$.

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, if $2x$ moles of $B$ are formed, then $x$ moles of $C$ are formed and $2x$ moles of $A$ are consumed.

Given $[B]_{eq} = 2x = 0.4$, so $x = 0.2 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$.

Equilibrium concentrations are:
$[A]_{eq} = 2.0 - 2x = 2.0 - 0.4 = 1.6 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$
$[B]_{eq} = 0.4 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$
$[C]_{eq} = x = 0.2 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$

The equilibrium constant $K_c$ is given by:
$K_c = \dfrac{[B]^2 [C]}{[A]^2}$

$K_c = \dfrac{(0.4)^2 \times (0.2)}{(1.6)^2}$

$K_c = \dfrac{0.16 \times 0.2}{2.56} = \dfrac{0.032}{2.56}$

$K_c = \dfrac{32 \times 10^{-3}}{2560 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{32}{2560} = \dfrac{1}{80} = 0.0125$

$K_c = 125 \times 10^{-4}$

Answer: 125

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The initial amount of 2 radioactive elements X and Y is 1 g each and their half-lives are 12 hours and 16 hours respectively. The ratio of X and Y after 2 days is:
questions.solution:
The amount of a radioactive substance remaining after time $t$ is given by $N(t) = N_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$, where $N_0$ is the initial amount and $T_{1/2}$ is the half-life.

Given $t = 2$ days = $48$ hours.

For element X: $N_0 = 1$ g, $T_{1/2} = 12$ hours. The number of half-lives is $n_X = \dfrac{48}{12} = 4$.

$N_X = 1 \times \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^{4} = \dfrac{1}{16}$ g.

For element Y: $N_0 = 1$ g, $T_{1/2} = 16$ hours. The number of half-lives is $n_Y = \dfrac{48}{16} = 3$.

$N_Y = 1 \times \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^{3} = \dfrac{1}{8}$ g.

The ratio of X to Y after 2 days is $\dfrac{N_X}{N_Y} = \dfrac{1/16}{1/8} = \dfrac{8}{16} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Answer: 1:2

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The concentration of the reactant $R$ with time $t$ for two different reactants (i) and (ii) are given in the plots. The respective orders of the reactants are:
questions.solution:
For a zero order reaction, the integrated rate law is given by $[R] = [R]_0 - kt$. A plot of $[R]$ versus time $t$ is a straight line with a negative slope equal to $-k$. This matches graph (i).

For a first order reaction, the integrated rate law is given by $\ln[R] = \ln[R]_0 - kt$. A plot of $\ln[R]$ versus time $t$ is a straight line with a negative slope equal to $-k$. This matches graph (ii).

Therefore, the order of reaction for graph (i) is 0 and for graph (ii) is 1.

Answer: 0,1

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
In the following reaction $x A \rightarrow y B$,
$\log _{10}\left[-\dfrac{d[A]}{d t}\right]=\log _{10}\left[\dfrac{d[B]}{d t}\right]+0.3010$

The relation between x and y is: [Given: $\log 2=0.3010, \log 4=0.6020$ ]
questions.solution:
For the reaction $x A \rightarrow y B$, the rate of reaction is given by:

$-\dfrac{1}{x} \dfrac{d[A]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{y} \dfrac{d[B]}{dt}$

This implies $-\dfrac{d[A]}{dt} = \dfrac{x}{y} \dfrac{d[B]}{dt}$

Taking $\log_{10}$ on both sides:

$\log_{10} \left( -\dfrac{d[A]}{dt} \right) = \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{x}{y} \dfrac{d[B]}{dt} \right)$

$\log_{10} \left( -\dfrac{d[A]}{dt} \right) = \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{d[B]}{dt} \right) + \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{x}{y} \right)$

Comparing this with the given equation $\log_{10} \left( -\dfrac{d[A]}{dt} \right) = \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{d[B]}{dt} \right) + 0.3010$, we get:

$\log_{10} \left( \dfrac{x}{y} \right) = 0.3010$

Since $0.3010 = \log_{10} 2$, we have:

$\log_{10} \left( \dfrac{x}{y} \right) = \log_{10} 2$

$\dfrac{x}{y} = 2 \Rightarrow x = 2y$

Answer: $x=2 y$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the two reactions, whose pre-exponential factor is same.
$\mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{700 \mathrm{~K}} \text { products }\mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[\text { catalyst }]{500 \mathrm{~K}} \text { products }$

In the presence of catalyst, it was found that the activation energy Ea is decreased by $30 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$ and the rate constant remains unchanged. The activation energy for the catalysed reaction is:
questions.solution:
The Arrhenius equation is given by $k = A e^{-E_a / (RT)}$.

For the uncatalyzed reaction at $T_1 = 700 \text{ K}$ with activation energy $E_{a1}$, the rate constant is $k_1 = A e^{-E_{a1} / (R \times 700)}$.

For the catalyzed reaction at $T_2 = 500 \text{ K}$ with activation energy $E_{a2}$, the rate constant is $k_2 = A e^{-E_{a2} / (R \times 500)}$.

Given that the rate constants are equal ($k_1 = k_2$) and the pre-exponential factor $A$ is the same, we have $e^{-E_{a1} / (700R)} = e^{-E_{a2} / (500R)}$.

Equating the exponents, $\dfrac{E_{a1}}{700} = \dfrac{E_{a2}}{500}$, which simplifies to $E_{a1} = \dfrac{7}{5} E_{a2} = 1.4 E_{a2}$.

It is given that the activation energy is decreased by $30 \text{ kJ/mol}$ in the presence of a catalyst, so $E_{a1} = E_{a2} + 30$.

Substituting $E_{a1}$ in the equation: $1.4 E_{a2} = E_{a2} + 30$.

$0.4 E_{a2} = 30$.

$E_{a2} = \dfrac{30}{0.4} = 75 \text{ kJ/mol}$.

Answer: $75 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The half- life of a first order reaction is ' $p$ ' and its $3 / 4^{\text {th }}$ life period is ' $q$ '. $p$ and $q$ are related to each other by: [Given: $\log 3=0.4771, \log 4=0.6040$ ]
questions.solution:
For a first order reaction, the rate constant $k$ is given by $k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{p}$, where $p$ is the half-life.

The $3/4^{\text{th}}$ life period $q$ is the time taken for the concentration to reduce to $1/4$ of its initial value. The integrated rate equation is $k = \dfrac{1}{q} \ln \left( \dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t} \right)$.

Substituting $[A]_t = \dfrac{1}{4}[A]_0$, we get $k = \dfrac{1}{q} \ln(4) = \dfrac{2 \ln 2}{q}$.

Equating the two expressions for $k$: $\dfrac{\ln 2}{p} = \dfrac{2 \ln 2}{q}$.

Simplifying this, we get $\dfrac{1}{p} = \dfrac{2}{q}$, which implies $q = 2p$ or $2p = q$.

Answer: $2 p=q$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Arrange the following ions in the decreasing order of their ionic radii: $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}, \mathrm{Ca}^{2+}, \mathrm{S}^{2-}, \mathrm{K}^{+}$
questions.solution:
The given ions are $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$, $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$, and $\mathrm{K}^{+}$.

First, determine the number of electrons in each ion:
$\mathrm{S}^{2-}$ has $16 + 2 = 18$ electrons.
$\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ has $17 + 1 = 18$ electrons.
$\mathrm{K}^{+}$ has $19 - 1 = 18$ electrons.
$\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ has $20 - 2 = 18$ electrons.

All these ions are isoelectronic, meaning they have the same number of electrons ($18$).

For isoelectronic species, the ionic radius decreases as the nuclear charge (atomic number, $Z$) increases, because a higher nuclear charge pulls the same number of electrons more strongly towards the nucleus.

The atomic numbers are:
$\mathrm{S} (Z = 16)$
$\mathrm{Cl} (Z = 17)$
$\mathrm{K} (Z = 19)$
$\mathrm{Ca} (Z = 20)$

Arranging them in decreasing order of ionic radii based on increasing atomic number:
$\mathrm{S}^{2-} (Z=16) \gt \mathrm{Cl}^{-} (Z=17) \gt \mathrm{K}^{+} (Z=19) \gt \mathrm{Ca}^{2+} (Z=20)$.

Answer: $\mathrm{S}^{2-} \gt \mathrm{Cl}^{-} \gt \mathrm{K}^{+} \gt \mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The number of geometrical isomers in the following metal complexes $\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO})_4,\left[\mathrm{Ru}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_3 \mathrm{Cl}_3\right],\left[\mathrm{CuCl}_2\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_4\right]^{+}$and $\left[\mathrm{PtCl}_2\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_2\right]$ are
questions.solution:
The complex $\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO})_4$ is a tetrahedral complex of the type $MA_4$. Tetrahedral complexes of the type $MA_4$ or $MA_3B$ do not exhibit geometrical isomerism. Thus, the number of geometrical isomers is $0$.

The complex $[\mathrm{Ru}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_3\mathrm{Cl}_3]$ is an octahedral complex of the type $MA_3B_3$. This type of complex exhibits two geometrical isomers: the facial (fac) isomer and the meridional (mer) isomer. Thus, the number of geometrical isomers is $2$.

The complex $[\mathrm{CuCl}_2(\mathrm{NH}_3)_4]^{+}$ is an octahedral complex of the type $MA_4B_2$. This type of complex exhibits two geometrical isomers: the trans isomer (where the two Cl ligands are at $180^{\circ}$) and the cis isomer (where the two Cl ligands are at $90^{\circ}$). Thus, the number of geometrical isomers is $2$.

The complex $[\mathrm{PtCl}_2(\mathrm{NH}_3)_2]$ is a square planar complex of the type $MA_2B_2$. This type of complex exhibits two geometrical isomers: the cis isomer and the trans isomer. Thus, the number of geometrical isomers is $2$.

The sequence of the number of geometrical isomers is $0, 2, 2, 2$.

Answer: $0,2,2,2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The wavelength absorbed by the complex $[Cu(H_2O)_4]^{2+}$ (assuming tetrahedral geometry) for the d-d transition is 600 nm. The crystal field splitting energy for the complex $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ is:
[Given: $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\text{ Js}$, $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ ms}^{-1}$, and $1\text{ eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$]
questions.solution:
Tetrahedral splitting energy:

$\Delta_t = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^8)}{600 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.313 \times 10^{-19}$ J

Since $\Delta_t = \dfrac{4}{9}\Delta_o$:

$\Delta_o = \dfrac{9}{4} \times 3.313 \times 10^{-19} = 7.454 \times 10^{-19}$ J

Converting to eV:

$\Delta_o = \dfrac{7.454 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 4.7$ eV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The 'd' electronic configuration of $\left[\mathrm{Ru}(\mathrm{en})_3\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2$ and $\left[\mathrm{Fe}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_6\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2$ respectively are _____ and ____ .
[Given: Atomic number of $\mathrm{Ru}=44$ and $\mathrm{Fe}=26$ ]
questions.solution:
For $\left[\mathrm{Ru}(\mathrm{en})_3\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2$, the oxidation state of $\mathrm{Ru}$ is $+2$. The atomic number of $\mathrm{Ru}$ is $44$, so its electronic configuration is $[\mathrm{Kr}] 4d^7 5s^1$. For $\mathrm{Ru}^{2+}$, the configuration is $4d^6$. Since $\mathrm{Ru}$ is a $4d$ transition metal, it forms low-spin complexes regardless of the ligand field strength. Thus, the $d^6$ configuration in an octahedral field results in $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$.

For $\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_6\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2$, the oxidation state of $\mathrm{Fe}$ is $+2$. The atomic number of $\mathrm{Fe}$ is $26$, so its electronic configuration is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3d^6 4s^2$. For $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$, the configuration is $3d^6$. Since $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$ is a weak field ligand, the complex is high-spin. The $d^6$ configuration in a high-spin octahedral field is $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$.

Therefore, the configurations are $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ and $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$.

Answer: $t_{2 g}{ }^6 e_g^0 ; t_{2 g}{ }^4 e_g^2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Choose the correct ascending order of the second ionisation enthalpies of the given metals.
A. $\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{Z}=26)$
B. $\mathrm{Mn}(Z=25)$
C. $V(Z=23)$
D. $\mathrm{Cr}(Z=24)$
questions.solution:
The second ionisation enthalpy involves the removal of an electron from the $M^{+}$ ion. The electronic configurations of the $M^{+}$ ions are as follows:

V ($Z=23$): $[Ar] 3d^3 4s^1$. Removing one electron gives $V^{+}$: $[Ar] 3d^3 4s^1$. The second ionisation involves removing the $4s^1$ electron.

Cr ($Z=24$): $[Ar] 3d^5 4s^1$. Removing one electron gives $Cr^{+}$: $[Ar] 3d^5$. The second ionisation involves removing an electron from the stable half-filled $3d^5$ subshell, which requires high energy.

Mn ($Z=25$): $[Ar] 3d^5 4s^2$. Removing one electron gives $Mn^{+}$: $[Ar] 3d^5 4s^1$. The second ionisation involves removing the $4s^1$ electron.

Fe ($Z=26$): $[Ar] 3d^6 4s^2$. Removing one electron gives $Fe^{+}$: $[Ar] 3d^6 4s^1$. The second ionisation involves removing the $4s^1$ electron.

Comparing the effective nuclear charge ($Z_{eff}$) for the removal of the $4s$ electron in V, Mn, and Fe, the energy increases as $Z$ increases: $V \lt Mn \lt Fe$.

For Cr, the second ionisation energy is exceptionally high because it requires breaking the stable $3d^5$ configuration. Thus, the order is $V \lt Mn \lt Fe \lt Cr$.

Matching this with the given options, $C \lt B \lt A \lt D$.

Answer: $\mathrm{C} \lt \mathrm{B} \lt \mathrm{A} \lt \mathrm{D}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In alkaline medium, $I^{-}$is oxidised to ' X ' by $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$. The oxidation state of iodine in ' X ' is:
questions.solution:
In alkaline medium, the reaction between permanganate ion and iodide ion is given by the balanced chemical equation:

2MnO_{4}^{-}$ + I$^{-}$ + H_{2}$O \rightarrow 2MnO_{2}$ + IO_{3}^{-}$ + 2OH$^{-}$

The product 'X' formed by the oxidation of I$^{-}$ is the iodate ion, IO_{3}^{-}$. \\ \\ To find the oxidation state of iodine in IO_{3}^{-}$, let the oxidation state be $x$.

$x + 3(-2) = -1$

$x - 6 = -1$

$x = +5$

Therefore, the oxidation state of iodine in 'X' is +5.

Answer: +5

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match the ions given in Column I with their characteristic properties given in Column II.
S.No.Column IS.No.Column II
A$Cr^{2+}$PStable in aqueous medium and has magnetic moment equal to 5.92 BM.
B$Cu^+$QOnly stable oxidation state and does not act as reducing agent.
C$Mn^{2+}$RIs a good reducing agent due to attainment of stable $d^3$ configuration.
D$Sc^{3+}$SUnstable in aqueous medium and readily disproportionates.
questions.solution:
For $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}$, the electronic configuration is $[Ar]3d^4$. It acts as a strong reducing agent because it gets oxidized to $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$ ($[Ar]3d^3$), which has a stable half-filled $t_{2g}$ subshell in octahedral fields. Thus, A matches R.

For $\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$, the electronic configuration is $[Ar]3d^{10}$. In aqueous solution, $\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$ is unstable and undergoes disproportionation to $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Cu}$. Thus, B matches S.

For $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$, the electronic configuration is $[Ar]3d^5$. It has 5 unpaired electrons, so the magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{5(7)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92$ BM. It is stable in aqueous medium. Thus, C matches P.

For $\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}$, the electronic configuration is $[Ar]3d^0$. It is the only stable oxidation state for scandium and does not act as a reducing agent as it has no electrons to lose. Thus, D matches Q.

Answer: $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{R} \quad \mathrm{B}=\mathrm{S}\quad \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{P}\quad \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{Q}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two statements, one Assertion and the other Reason, are given. Choose the right option.
Assertion: The Standard Electrode potential, $\mathrm{E}^0 \mathrm{Co}^{3+} / \mathrm{Co}^{2+}$ is greater than $\mathrm{E}^0 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+} / \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$.
Reason: $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ ions are less stable in aqueous medium than $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions which has stable $\mathrm{d}^5$ configuration
options: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
questions.solution:
The standard electrode potential $E^{0}$ for the reduction $M^{3+} + e^{-} \rightarrow M^{2+}$ depends on the stability of the $M^{3+}$ and $M^{2+}$ oxidation states in aqueous solution. For iron, the $Fe^{3+}$ ion has a stable $d^{5}$ configuration, making it relatively stable compared to $Fe^{2+}$ ($d^{6}$), resulting in a lower reduction potential of $+0.77$ V.

For cobalt, the $Co^{3+}$ ion has a $d^{6}$ configuration and is a strong oxidizing agent because it is highly unstable in aqueous medium compared to $Co^{2+}$ ($d^{7}$), which is more stable. Consequently, the reduction potential $E^{0} Co^{3+} / Co^{2+}$ is significantly higher, approximately $+1.97$ V.

Since the reduction potential of $Co^{3+} / Co^{2+}$ is greater than that of $Fe^{3+} / Fe^{2+}$, the Assertion is correct. The Reason correctly identifies that $Co^{3+}$ is less stable in aqueous medium than $Fe^{3+}$ (which has a stable $d^{5}$ configuration), and this difference in stability is the fundamental cause for the difference in their reduction potentials. Thus, the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A current of 0.10 A was passed for 2 hours through a dilute solution of sulphuric acid. The total volume of gaseous products produced at STP is:
[Given: $1 \mathrm{~F}=96500 \mathrm{C}$; Molar volume at STP is $22.7 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ]
questions.solution:
The electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid involves the electrolysis of water. The reactions at the electrodes are as follows:

At cathode: $4H^{+}(aq) + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_{2}(g)$

At anode: $2H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow O_{2}(g) + 4H^{+}(aq) + 4e^{-}$

The total charge passed $Q$ is given by $Q = I \times t = 0.10 \text{ A} \times (2 \times 3600 \text{ s}) = 720 \text{ C}$.

The number of moles of electrons passed is $n_{e} = \dfrac{Q}{F} = \dfrac{720}{96500} \approx 0.00746 \text{ mol}$.

From the stoichiometry, $4$ moles of electrons produce $2$ moles of $H_{2}$ and $1$ mole of $O_{2}$, totaling $3$ moles of gas. Thus, $4$ moles of electrons produce $3$ moles of gas.

Total moles of gas produced $n_{total} = \dfrac{3}{4} \times n_{e} = 0.75 \times 0.00746 = 0.005595 \text{ mol}$.

The volume of gas at STP is $V = n_{total} \times 22.7 \text{ L/mol} = 0.005595 \times 22.7 \approx 0.1270 \text{ L}$.

Converting to mL, $V = 0.1270 \times 1000 = 127 \text{ mL}$.

Answer: 127 mL

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify the two statements which are incorrect regarding Corrosion of Iron.
A. During electrical protection of underground Iron pipes from corrosion the connected Mg plate undergoes reduction.
B. At the Cathodic area on Iron the reaction occurring is $4 \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{O}_2+4 \mathrm{e} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$
C. Rust formed $\mathrm{Fe}_2 \mathrm{O}_3 . \mathrm{xH}_2 \mathrm{O}$ is an acidic oxide.
D. The $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions are obtained from water containing dissolved gases like $\mathrm{SO}_2, \mathrm{NO}_2$ or $\mathrm{CO}_2$.
questions.solution:
In the process of cathodic protection of iron pipes, a more reactive metal like magnesium is used as a sacrificial anode. The magnesium undergoes oxidation ($Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^{-}$) to protect the iron. Therefore, statement A is incorrect because Mg undergoes oxidation, not reduction.

At the cathodic area of iron corrosion, oxygen is reduced in the presence of moisture. The reaction is $O_2 + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2H_2O$. This is a standard cathodic reaction in acidic or neutral media, making statement B correct.

Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, $\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3 \cdot x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$. Iron(III) oxide is a basic oxide, not an acidic oxide. Therefore, statement C is incorrect.

The presence of dissolved acidic gases like $\mathrm{SO}_2$, $\mathrm{NO}_2$, or $\mathrm{CO}_2$ in water increases the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ ions, which accelerates the corrosion process. Thus, statement D is correct.

Since statements A and C are incorrect, the correct option is A & C.

Answer: A & C

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the cell
$\mathrm{Pt}\left|\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{~g})(1 \mathrm{bar})\right| \mathrm{H}^{+}(\mathrm{aq}) \| \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) \mid \mathrm{Cu}$

At 298 K , the emf of the cell is 0.31 V . The pH of the acidic solution is 3 . The concentration of $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ is:
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $\mathrm{H}_2(g) + \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}^{+}(aq) + \mathrm{Cu}(s)$.

The standard cell potential $E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cathode} - E^{\circ}_{anode} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{H}^{+}/\mathrm{H}_2} = 0.34 \mathrm{V} - 0.00 \mathrm{V} = 0.34 \mathrm{V}$.

Using the Nernst equation at 298 K:

$E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log Q$

Here $n = 2$, $Q = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H}^{+}]^2}{P_{\mathrm{H}_2} [\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$. Given $\mathrm{pH} = 3$, so $[\mathrm{H}^{+}] = 10^{-3} \mathrm{M}$. $P_{\mathrm{H}_2} = 1 \mathrm{bar}$.

$0.31 = 0.34 - \dfrac{0.0591}{2} \log \left( \dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{1 \times [\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]} \right)$

$-0.03 = -0.02955 \log \left( \dfrac{10^{-6}}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]} \right)$

Approximating $0.0591/2 \approx 0.03$, we get $1 \approx \log \left( \dfrac{10^{-6}}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]} \right)$.

Therefore, $10^1 = \dfrac{10^{-6}}{[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}]}$, which implies $[\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}] = 10^{-7} \mathrm{M}$.

Answer: $10^{-7} \mathrm{M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
In the reaction,
$F e_{(a q)}^{2+}+A g_{(a q)}^{+} \rightarrow F e_{(a q)}^{3+}+A g_{(s)}$

The standard emf $\left(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}\right)$ of the cell is:
$\left[\right.$ Given: $\left.E_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+} / \mathrm{Ag}}^o=a V ; \quad E_{\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} / \mathrm{Fe}}^o=b V ; E_{\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} / \mathrm{Fe}}^o=c V\right]$
questions.solution:
Oxidation (Anode): $Fe^{2+} \to Fe^{3+} + e^-$
Reduction (Cathode): $Ag^+ + e^- \to Ag$

$E°_{cell} = E°_{cathode} - E°_{anode} = E°_{Ag^+/Ag} - E°_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$

Finding $E°_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$ using Gibbs free energy:

Reaction 1: $Fe^{2+} + 2e^- \to Fe$, $E°_1 = b$, $\Delta G°_1 = -2Fb$
Reaction 2: $Fe^{3+} + 3e^- \to Fe$, $E°_2 = c$, $\Delta G°_2 = -3Fc$

Target (Reaction 2 $-$ Reaction 1): $Fe^{3+} + e^- \to Fe^{2+}$

$\Delta G°_3 = \Delta G°_2 - \Delta G°_1 = -3Fc - (-2Fb) = -3Fc + 2Fb$

$-1 \cdot F \cdot E°_3 = -3Fc + 2Fb \Rightarrow E°_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = 3c - 2b$

$E°_{cell} = a - (3c - 2b) = a + 2b - 3c$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The variation of the molar conductivity with concentration of an electrolyte $(X)$ in aqueous solution is shown in the given figure.
The electrolyte ' X ' is:
questions.solution:
The graph shows the variation of molar conductivity ($\lambda_m$) with the square root of concentration ($\sqrt{c}$).

For strong electrolytes like $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{KCl}$, and $\text{HNO}_3$, the molar conductivity increases linearly with decreasing concentration according to the Kohlrausch equation: $\lambda_m = \lambda_m^0 - A\sqrt{c}$. These electrolytes show a gradual increase in $\lambda_m$ as concentration decreases, and they can be extrapolated to infinite dilution to find $\lambda_m^0$.

For weak electrolytes like $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, the molar conductivity increases sharply as the concentration decreases, especially at very low concentrations. This is due to the increase in the degree of dissociation of the weak electrolyte as the solution is diluted. The curve for a weak electrolyte does not show a linear relationship with $\sqrt{c}$ and cannot be extrapolated to infinite dilution to determine $\lambda_m^0$.

The provided graph exhibits a sharp increase in $\lambda_m$ as $\sqrt{c}$ approaches zero, which is characteristic of a weak electrolyte. Among the given options, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is the only weak electrolyte.

Answer: $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}$

questions.solution:

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following is not aromatic?
questions.solution:
Aromatic compounds must satisfy Huckel's rule, which states that a planar, cyclic, conjugated system must have $(4n + 2)\pi$ electrons to be aromatic, where $n$ is an integer.

Cyclopentadienyl anion has $6\pi$ electrons ($4$ from two double bonds and $2$ from the lone pair on the carbon atom), which satisfies $4n + 2 = 6$ for $n = 1$. Thus, it is aromatic.

Pyridine is a heterocyclic aromatic compound with $6\pi$ electrons ($6$ from the ring atoms), satisfying Huckel's rule. Thus, it is aromatic.

Cyclopropenyl cation has $2\pi$ electrons from the one double bond, which satisfies $4n + 2 = 2$ for $n = 0$. Thus, it is aromatic.

Cyclooctatetraene has $8\pi$ electrons. According to Huckel's rule, systems with $4n$ electrons are anti-aromatic if planar. However, cyclooctatetraene adopts a non-planar tub-shaped conformation to avoid anti-aromaticity, making it non-aromatic.

Answer: Cyclooctatetraene

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following exhibits geometrical isomerism?
questions.solution:
Geometrical isomerism occurs in alkenes when each carbon atom of the double bond is attached to two different groups. Let us examine the structures of the given compounds.

For 1, 2-dibromopropene, the structure is $CH_3-C(Br)=CHBr$. The carbon at position 2 is attached to a methyl group and a bromine atom. The carbon at position 1 is attached to a hydrogen atom and a bromine atom. Since both carbons have two different groups attached, this compound exhibits geometrical isomerism (cis and trans forms).

For 2-methylbut-2-ene, the structure is $(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_3$. The carbon at position 2 is attached to two identical methyl groups, so it does not exhibit geometrical isomerism.

For hex-1-ene, the structure is $CH_2=CHCH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3$. The terminal carbon is attached to two identical hydrogen atoms, so it does not exhibit geometrical isomerism.

For 1, 1-diphenylethene, the structure is $(C_6H_5)_2C=CH_2$. The carbon at position 1 is attached to two identical phenyl groups, so it does not exhibit geometrical isomerism.

Answer: 1, 2-Dibromopropene

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the incorrect statement
options: In organic compounds resonance effect operates only in unsaturated compounds and results in delocalisation of electrons.
Larger the number of methyl groups linked to the doubly bonded Carbon atoms, greater is the stability of the alkene.

The Prussian blue precipitate formed during Lassaigne's test for detection of Nitrogen in an organic compound is due to formation of $\mathrm{Fe}_4\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right]_2 \times \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$
In the Carius method for estimation of halogens in an organic compound, the compound is heated with fuming nitric acid in presence of $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$.
questions.solution:
(1) Correct: Resonance effect involves delocalization of $\pi$-electrons or lone pairs, requiring unsaturated or conjugated systems.

(2) Correct: More alkyl (methyl) groups on doubly bonded carbons increase stability via hyperconjugation.

(3) Incorrect: The correct formula for Prussian blue is $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3 \cdot xH_2O$. The formula given in option (3) has the wrong subscript (2 instead of 3) for the hexacyanoferrate ion.

(4) Correct: In the Carius method, the organic compound is heated with fuming nitric acid in presence of $AgNO_3$ to convert halogens into measurable silver halide precipitate.

The incorrect statement is (3).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify the product formed when the following reaction occurs.
?
questions.solution:
The reaction of ethylbenzene with excess $Cl_2$ in the presence of $hv$ (ultraviolet light) is a free radical substitution reaction. The reaction occurs at the benzylic position because the resulting benzylic radical is resonance-stabilized by the benzene ring.

The first step involves the abstraction of a hydrogen atom from the benzylic carbon ($CH_2$) to form a 1-phenylethyl radical, which then reacts with $Cl_2$ to form 1-chloro-1-phenylethane.

Since the reagent $Cl_2$ is in excess, the reaction continues at the same benzylic position. The hydrogen atom remaining on the benzylic carbon is abstracted to form a 1-chloro-1-phenylethyl radical, which is further stabilized by both the phenyl ring and the chlorine atom. This radical then reacts with another molecule of $Cl_2$ to form 1,1-dichloro-1-phenylethane.

Therefore, the major product formed under conditions of excess chlorine is 1,1-dichloro-1-phenylethane.

Answer: 1, 1-Dichloro-1-phenylethane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order towards $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}} 1$ reactions.
questions.solution:
The rate of an $S_{N}1$ reaction depends on the stability of the carbocation intermediate formed after the departure of the leaving group (bromide ion). The more stable the carbocation, the faster the $S_{N}1$ reaction.

The carbocations formed from the given compounds are:
(I) Benzyl carbocation: $C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}^{+}$, which is stabilized by resonance with one phenyl ring.
(II) Diphenylmethyl carbocation: $(C_{6}H_{5})_{2}CH^{+}$, which is stabilized by resonance with two phenyl rings.
(III) 1-Phenylethyl carbocation: $C_{6}H_{5}CH(CH_{3})^{+}$, which is stabilized by resonance with one phenyl ring and the inductive effect of the methyl group.
(IV) 1,1-Diphenylethyl carbocation: $(C_{6}H_{5})_{2}C(CH_{3})^{+}$, which is stabilized by resonance with two phenyl rings and the inductive effect of the methyl group.

Comparing the stabilities:
1. Compound (I) forms a primary benzylic carbocation (least stable among the options).
2. Compound (III) forms a secondary benzylic carbocation, which is more stable than (I) due to the electron-donating methyl group.
3. Compound (II) forms a secondary carbocation stabilized by two phenyl rings, which is more stable than (III).
4. Compound (IV) forms a tertiary carbocation stabilized by two phenyl rings and one methyl group, making it the most stable.

The order of stability of carbocations is (I) < (III) < (II) < (IV).

Therefore, the increasing order of reactivity towards $S_{N}1$ reactions is (I) < (III) < (II) < (IV).

Answer: I $ \lt $ III $ \lt $ II $ \lt $ IV

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Consider the following compounds , $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{Cl}(\mathrm{A}), \quad \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{Br}(\mathrm{B}), \quad \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{Br}_2(\mathrm{C}), \quad \mathrm{CHBr}_3(\mathrm{D})$ The correct order of boiling points of the compounds is:
questions.solution:
The boiling point of haloalkanes depends primarily on the molecular mass and the strength of intermolecular forces, specifically dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces. As the molecular mass increases, the magnitude of van der Waals forces increases, leading to higher boiling points.

Comparing the compounds:
(A) $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Cl}$: Molecular mass $\approx 15 + 35.5 = 50.5$ u
(B) $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Br}$: Molecular mass $\approx 15 + 80 = 95$ u
(C) $\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br}_2$: Molecular mass $\approx 14 + 160 = 174$ u
(D) $\mathrm{CHBr}_3$: Molecular mass $\approx 13 + 240 = 253$ u

Since the molecular mass increases in the order $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Cl} \lt \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Br} \lt \mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br}_2 \lt \mathrm{CHBr}_3$, the boiling points follow the same trend. Therefore, the order is $\mathrm{D} \gt \mathrm{C} \gt \mathrm{B} \gt \mathrm{A}$.

Answer: D $ \gt $ C $ \gt $ B $ \gt $ A

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following reaction can be used for the preparation of flouromethane?
questions.solution:
The preparation of alkyl fluorides from alkyl halides is typically achieved using the Swarts reaction. In this reaction, an alkyl bromide or alkyl chloride is treated with a metallic fluoride such as $\mathrm{AgF}$, $\mathrm{Hg}_2\mathrm{F}_2$, or $\mathrm{CoF}_2$.

The reaction is represented as: $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Br} + \mathrm{AgF} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{F} + \mathrm{AgBr}$.

The other options are not suitable for the preparation of fluoromethane: $\mathrm{CH}_4 + \mathrm{F}_2$ is an extremely violent and uncontrolled free-radical substitution reaction, while $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{OH} + \mathrm{HF}$ and $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{NH}_2 + \mathrm{HF}$ do not undergo simple nucleophilic substitution to yield fluoromethane under standard laboratory conditions.

Answer: $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{Br}+\mathrm{AgF} \longrightarrow$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the following reaction
$\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_6+\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{Br} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text { anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl}_3} \mathrm{X}$

The major product ' X ' is:
questions.solution:
The reaction given is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation reaction.

Benzene ($\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6$) reacts with ethyl bromide ($\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br}$) in the presence of an anhydrous Lewis acid catalyst, $\mathrm{AlCl}_3$.

The mechanism involves the formation of an electrophile, the ethyl carbocation ($\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2^{+}$), which then undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution on the benzene ring.

The reaction is: $\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6 + \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl}_3} \mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3 + \mathrm{HBr}$.

The product $\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3$ is ethylbenzene.

Answer: Ethylbenzene

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The major product of acid catalysed hydration reaction of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene is:
questions.solution:
The acid-catalyzed hydration of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene proceeds via the formation of a carbocation intermediate. The reaction begins with the protonation of the double bond to form the more stable carbocation. Protonation of the terminal carbon of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene yields a secondary carbocation, $(CH_3)_3C-CH^{+}-CH_3$.

This secondary carbocation undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to form a more stable tertiary carbocation, $(CH_3)_2C^{+}-CH(CH_3)_2$. This rearrangement is driven by the conversion of a secondary carbocation into a more stable tertiary carbocation.

Subsequently, a water molecule acts as a nucleophile and attacks the tertiary carbocation to form the corresponding oxonium ion. Deprotonation of the oxonium ion yields the final product, 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol.

Answer: 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: According to the decreasing order of reactivity towards electrophilic substitutions, which of the following is incorrect?
questions.solution:
Reactivity towards electrophilic aromatic substitution is determined by the electron density of the benzene ring. Substituents that increase electron density (electron-donating groups, EDG) activate the ring, while substituents that decrease electron density (electron-withdrawing groups, EWG) deactivate the ring.

Option (1): The order given is Toluene > Phenol > Benzene > p-Chlorobenzoic acid. This is incorrect because phenol (with a strong +M effect) is significantly more reactive than toluene (with a +I and hyperconjugation effect). The correct order should be Phenol > Toluene > Benzene > p-Chlorobenzoic acid.

Option (2): The order given is Toluene > Chlorobenzene > p-Nitrochlorobenzene > 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene. This is correct as the reactivity decreases with the addition of more electron-withdrawing nitro groups.

Option (3): The order given is Toluene > Benzene > Chlorobenzene > Nitrobenzene. This is correct as the methyl group activates the ring, while chlorine and the nitro group deactivate it, with the nitro group being a much stronger deactivator.

Option (4): The order given is Anisole > Toluene > Benzene > Benzotrifluoride. This is correct as the methoxy group is a strong activator (+M), the methyl group is a weak activator, and the trifluoromethyl group is a strong deactivator (-I).

Since the question asks for the incorrect order, option (1) is the correct choice.

Answer:

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the following reaction
$\mathrm{X} \xrightarrow[\text { (ii) } \mathrm{Zn} / \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}]{\text { (i) } \mathrm{O}_3} \text { 5-keto-2-methylhexanal }$

The reactant ' X ' is:
questions.solution:
Reductive ozonolysis cleaves the $C=C$ bond and replaces it with two carbonyl groups. To find X, we perform reverse ozonolysis on the product.

Product: 5-keto-2-methylhexanal

$O=CH-CH(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2-C(=O)-CH_3$

The two carbonyl carbons are C1 (aldehyde) and C5 (ketone). Joining C1 and C5 forms a 5-membered ring with a $C=C$ between them.

Substituents on the ring: C5 carries a $CH_3$ (C6), and C2 carries a $CH_3$.

Numbering to give lowest locants \rightarrow methyl groups at positions 1 and 3.

X is 1,3-dimethylcyclopentene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
A buffer solution was prepared by mixing 5 g of acetic acid with 7.5 g of sodium acetate. The solution was made upto 500 mL . The pH of the resulting solution is:
$\left[p K_a=4.76\right]$
questions.solution:
The molar mass of acetic acid ($CH_{3}COOH$) is $60\text{ g/mol}$. The number of moles of acetic acid is $n_{acid} = \dfrac{5}{60} = \dfrac{1}{12}\text{ mol}$.

The molar mass of sodium acetate ($CH_{3}COONa$) is $82\text{ g/mol}$. The number of moles of sodium acetate is $n_{salt} = \dfrac{7.5}{82} \approx 0.09146\text{ mol}$.

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer: $pH = pK_{a} + \log \left( \dfrac{[salt]}{[acid]} \right)$.

Since the volume is the same for both components in the $500\text{ mL}$ solution, the ratio of concentrations is equal to the ratio of moles: $pH = pK_{a} + \log \left( \dfrac{n_{salt}}{n_{acid}} \right)$.

$pH = 4.76 + \log \left( \dfrac{7.5/82}{5/60} \right) = 4.76 + \log \left( \dfrac{7.5}{82} \times \dfrac{60}{5} \right) = 4.76 + \log \left( \dfrac{1.5 \times 60}{82} \right) = 4.76 + \log \left( \dfrac{90}{82} \right)$.

$pH = 4.76 + \log(1.0976) \approx 4.76 + 0.04 = 4.8$.

Answer: 4.8

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which among the following species does not exhibit disproportionation reaction?
questions.solution:
A disproportionation reaction occurs when an element in an intermediate oxidation state is simultaneously oxidized and reduced. For a species to undergo disproportionation, the central atom must be in an oxidation state that is neither its maximum nor its minimum possible oxidation state.

Calculate the oxidation state of Bromine (Br) in each species:

In $\mathrm{BrO}_4^{-}$, let the oxidation state of Br be $x$. Then $x + 4(-2) = -1$, which gives $x = +7$. The maximum oxidation state of Bromine is $+7$ (group 17). Since it is already in its maximum oxidation state, it cannot be further oxidized. Therefore, $\mathrm{BrO}_4^{-}$ cannot undergo disproportionation.

In $\mathrm{BrO}_2^{-}$, $x + 2(-2) = -1$, so $x = +3$. This is an intermediate oxidation state, so it can disproportionate.

In $\mathrm{BrO}^{-}$, $x + (-2) = -1$, so $x = +1$. This is an intermediate oxidation state, so it can disproportionate.

In $\mathrm{BrO}_3^{-}$, $x + 3(-2) = -1$, so $x = +5$. This is an intermediate oxidation state, so it can disproportionate.

Answer: $\mathrm{BrO}_4^{-}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For the reaction,
$2 \mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}+b \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-}+c \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow x \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+y \mathrm{CO}_2+z \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$

Find $b, c, x, y$ and $z$
questions.solution:
The given redox reaction is $2 \mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + b \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-} + c \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow x \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + y \mathrm{CO}_2 + z \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$.

The oxidation half-reaction is $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_2 + 2e^{-}$.

The reduction half-reaction is $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + 8 \mathrm{H}^{+} + 5e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 4 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$.

To balance the electrons, multiply the oxidation half-reaction by 5 and the reduction half-reaction by 2:

$5 \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 10 \mathrm{CO}_2 + 10e^{-}$

$2 \mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + 16 \mathrm{H}^{+} + 10e^{-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 8 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$

Adding the two half-reactions gives:

$2 \mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + 5 \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-} + 16 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 10 \mathrm{CO}_2 + 8 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$

Comparing this with the given equation, we find $b=5$, $c=16$, $x=2$, $y=10$, and $z=8$.

Answer: $b=5, \quad c=16, \quad x=2, \quad y=10, \quad z=8$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: At $298 \mathrm{~K}, \mathrm{CO}_2$ exerts a partial pressure of 0.835 bar. The amount of $\mathrm{CO}_2$ in millimoles dissolved in 0.9 L of water is: $\left[\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{H}}\right.$ for $\mathrm{CO}_2$ at 298 K is $\left.1.67 \times 10^3 \mathrm{bar}\right]$
questions.solution:
Henry's Law states that the partial pressure of a gas is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: $P = K_H \times \chi$.

Given $P = 0.835 \text{ bar}$ and $K_H = 1.67 \times 10^3 \text{ bar}$, the mole fraction $\chi$ of $\text{CO}_2$ is calculated as:

$\chi = \dfrac{P}{K_H} = \dfrac{0.835}{1.67 \times 10^3} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} = 5 \times 10^{-4}$.

The mole fraction $\chi$ is defined as $\chi = \dfrac{n_{\text{CO}_2}}{n_{\text{CO}_2} + n_{\text{H}_2\text{O}}}$. Since the amount of dissolved gas is very small, $n_{\text{CO}_2} + n_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \approx n_{\text{H}_2\text{O}}$.

The number of moles of water in $0.9 \text{ L}$ is $n_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = \dfrac{900 \text{ g}}{18 \text{ g/mol}} = 50 \text{ mol}$.

Therefore, $n_{\text{CO}_2} = \chi \times n_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \times 50 = 250 \times 10^{-4} = 0.025 \text{ mol}$.

Converting to millimoles: $0.025 \text{ mol} = 25 \text{ mmol}$.

Answer: 25 mmol

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Choose the correct answer from the options given below.

Assertion (A): The molality of KCl solution at 25°C is 5 m. (Given molar mass of KCl is 74.5 g/mol). When the solution is cooled to -10°C, the molality of the solution remains unchanged.
Reason (R): The molality of the solution does not change with temperature as the mass remains unaffected with temperature.
options: Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$
A is false but R is true
Both $A$ and $R$ are true, $R$ is the correct explanation of $A$
questions.solution:
Molality $= \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}$

Since mass is independent of temperature (unlike volume), molality does not change with temperature. So Reason (R) is true.

A 5 m KCl solution has a highly depressed freezing point ($\approx -18.6°C$), so it remains liquid at $-10°C$ and its molality stays unchanged. So Assertion (A) is also true.

R correctly explains A, hence both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two liquids A and B form an ideal solution. At 300 K , the vapour pressure of pure A and pure B are $8 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~Pa}$ and $12 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~Pa}$ respectively. If the solution has 40 mole percent of $A$, the composition of $A$ and $B$ in the vapour phase is:
questions.solution:
Given the mole fraction of A in the liquid phase $x_A = 0.40$.

Since the solution is ideal, the mole fraction of B in the liquid phase is $x_B = 1 - x_A = 1 - 0.40 = 0.60$.

The vapour pressures of pure components are $P_A^{0} = 8 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$ and $P_B^{0} = 12 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$.

The partial pressures of A and B in the vapour phase are given by Raoult's Law:
$P_A = x_A P_A^{0} = 0.40 \times 8 \times 10^3 = 3.2 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$
$P_B = x_B P_B^{0} = 0.60 \times 12 \times 10^3 = 7.2 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$

The total vapour pressure $P_{total} = P_A + P_B = 3.2 \times 10^3 + 7.2 \times 10^3 = 10.4 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$.

The mole fraction of A in the vapour phase $y_A$ is given by:
$y_A = \dfrac{P_A}{P_{total}} = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^3}{10.4 \times 10^3} = \dfrac{3.2}{10.4} = \dfrac{32}{104} = \dfrac{4}{13} \approx 0.3077$.

The mole fraction of B in the vapour phase $y_B$ is given by:
$y_B = 1 - y_A = 1 - 0.3077 = 0.6923$.

Rounding to two decimal places, $y_A \approx 0.30$ and $y_B \approx 0.70$.

Answer: 0.30 and 0.70

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
0.60 g of urea is dissolved in 360 g of water at room temperature. The vapour pressure of pure water is 35 mm of Hg , the lowering of vapour pressure at this temperature is:
[Molar mass of urea is $60 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ]
questions.solution:
The molar mass of urea is $M_{urea} = 60 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$. The mass of urea is $w_{urea} = 0.60 \text{ g}$.

The number of moles of urea is $n_{urea} = \dfrac{0.60}{60} = 0.01 \text{ mol}$.

The mass of water is $w_{water} = 360 \text{ g}$. The molar mass of water is $M_{water} = 18 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

The number of moles of water is $n_{water} = \dfrac{360}{18} = 20 \text{ mol}$.

According to Raoult's law, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is given by $\dfrac{P^0 - P_s}{P^0} = \dfrac{n_{urea}}{n_{urea} + n_{water}}$.

Substituting the values, $\dfrac{P^0 - P_s}{35} = \dfrac{0.01}{0.01 + 20} = \dfrac{0.01}{20.01} \approx \dfrac{0.01}{20} = 0.0005$.

The lowering of vapour pressure is $P^0 - P_s = 35 \times 0.0005 = 0.0175 \text{ mm of Hg}$.

Rounding to the nearest given option, the value is $0.017 \text{ mm of Hg}$.

Answer: 0.017 mm of Hg

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: 800 mL of a $0.5 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{HNO}_3$ at 300 K is heated to a temperature of 350 K , its volume is reduced to one half and 10.5 g of $\mathrm{HNO}_3$ is evaporated. Assuming complete ionization, the osmotic pressure of the remaining solution is: [Given $\mathrm{R}=0.082 \mathrm{~L} \mathrm{~atm} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ]
questions.solution:
Initial moles of $HNO_3$: $n_1 = 0.5 \times 0.8 = 0.4$ mol

Moles evaporated: $n_{evap} = \dfrac{10.5}{63} = \dfrac{1}{6}$ mol

Remaining moles: $n_2 = 0.4 - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{12}{30} - \dfrac{5}{30} = \dfrac{7}{30}$ mol

Final volume: $V_2 = \dfrac{800}{2} = 400$ mL $= 0.4$ L

Final molarity: $C_2 = \dfrac{7/30}{0.4} = \dfrac{7}{12}$ M

$HNO_3 \to H^+ + NO_3^-$, so van't Hoff factor $i = 2$

$\pi = i \cdot C_2 \cdot R \cdot T = 2 \times \dfrac{7}{12} \times 0.082 \times 350 = \dfrac{7}{6} \times 28.7 = \dfrac{200.9}{6} \approx 33.5$ atm

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: 20 g of $\mathrm{N}_2$ is made to react with 5 g of $\mathrm{H}_2$ to give ammonia. The limiting reagent and number of moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ formed respectively are:
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the formation of ammonia is: $\mathrm{N}_2(g) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_3(g)$.

Calculate the initial moles of reactants:
Moles of $\mathrm{N}_2 = \dfrac{20 \text{ g}}{28 \text{ g/mol}} = 0.714 \text{ moles}$.
Moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 = \dfrac{5 \text{ g}}{2 \text{ g/mol}} = 2.5 \text{ moles}$.

Determine the limiting reagent:
According to the stoichiometry, 1 mole of $\mathrm{N}_2$ requires 3 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2$.
For 0.714 moles of $\mathrm{N}_2$, the required $\mathrm{H}_2 = 0.714 \times 3 = 2.142 \text{ moles}$.
Since the available $\mathrm{H}_2$ (2.5 moles) is greater than the required amount (2.142 moles), $\mathrm{N}_2$ is the limiting reagent.

Calculate the moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ formed:
From the stoichiometry, 1 mole of $\mathrm{N}_2$ produces 2 moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$.
Therefore, 0.714 moles of $\mathrm{N}_2$ will produce $0.714 \times 2 = 1.428 \text{ moles}$ of $\mathrm{NH}_3$.

Rounding to two decimal places, the moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ formed is 1.43 moles.

Answer: $\mathrm{N}_2$ and 1.43 moles

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass 6.63 g moving with a velocity of $100 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ is:
questions.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ is given by the formula $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $m$ is the mass of the particle, and $v$ is its velocity.

Given values are:
$h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$
$m = 6.63 \text{ g} = 6.63 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$
$v = 100 \text{ m s}^{-1} = 10^{2} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Substituting these values into the formula:
$\lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{(6.63 \times 10^{-3}) \times 10^{2}}$

$\lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{6.63 \times 10^{-1}}$

$\lambda = 10^{-34 - (-1)} = 10^{-33} \text{ m}$

Answer: $10^{-33} \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify the incorrect statement/s.
A. The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in an atom, in which the largest Principal quantum number value is 4 , is 54 . B. According to Rydberg, all series of lines in Hydrogen spectrum can be described by the equation:
$\dfrac{1}{\lambda}=109677\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2}-\dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right) \mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ where $\left(n_1 \lt n_2\right)$
questions.solution:
For statement A, the maximum number of electrons in an atom with principal quantum number $n=4$ is determined by the total number of orbitals available. The orbitals are $1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 3d, 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f$. The number of orbitals is $1 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 5 + 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 30$. Each orbital can hold 2 electrons, so the maximum capacity is $30 \times 2 = 60$ electrons. Thus, statement A is incorrect.

For statement B, the Rydberg formula for the hydrogen spectrum is given by $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H \left( \dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} \right)$, where $R_H \approx 109677 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. This equation describes all series of lines in the hydrogen spectrum for $n_1 \lt n_2$. Thus, statement B is correct.

Answer: Only A

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The enthalpy change accompanying the freezing of 18 g of water at $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to ice at $-5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is:
[Given: $\Delta H_{(\text {fusion })}=6 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} ; \quad C_p\left(H_2 \mathrm{O}, l\right)=75.3 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} ; \quad C_p\left(H_2 \mathrm{O}, s\right)=36.8 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ]
questions.solution:
The process of freezing 18 g (1 mole) of water at $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to ice at $-5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ can be broken down into three steps:

Cooling 1 mole of liquid water from $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$\Delta H_1 = n C_p(l) \Delta T = 1 \times 75.3 \times (0 - 5) \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kJ} = -0.3765 \mathrm{~kJ}$

Phase change of 1 mole of liquid water at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to ice at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$\Delta H_2 = -\Delta H_{\text{fusion}} = -6.0 \mathrm{~kJ}$

Cooling 1 mole of ice from $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $-5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
$\Delta H_3 = n C_p(s) \Delta T = 1 \times 36.8 \times (-5 - 0) \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kJ} = -0.184 \mathrm{~kJ}$

Total enthalpy change $\Delta H = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3 = -0.3765 - 6.0 - 0.184 = -6.5605 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.

Answer: $-6.56 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ were found to be both positive for a reversible reaction at temperature ' T '. If the equilibrium temperature is $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{o}}$, the reaction will be spontaneous when
options: $T_o$ should be double than that of T
questions.solution:
For a reaction to be spontaneous, the change in Gibbs free energy must be negative, i.e., $\Delta G \lt 0$.

The relationship between Gibbs free energy, enthalpy, and entropy is given by the equation $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$.

At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$, which implies $\Delta H - T_o\Delta S = 0$. Therefore, the equilibrium temperature is $T_o = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$.

For the reaction to be spontaneous, $\Delta H - T\Delta S \lt 0$.

Since $\Delta H \gt 0$ and $\Delta S \gt 0$, we have $\Delta H \lt T\Delta S$, which simplifies to $T \gt \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$.

Substituting the expression for $T_o$, we get $T \gt T_o$.

Answer: $T \gt T_o$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When the combustion of one molecule of liquid heptane is carried out at a constant temperature ' $T$ ', the difference between $\Delta H^o$ and $\Delta U^o$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
The combustion reaction of liquid heptane ($C_{7}H_{16}$) is given by:

$C_{7}H_{16}(l) + 11O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 7CO_{2}(g) + 8H_{2}O(l)$

The relationship between enthalpy change ($\Delta H^{o}$) and internal energy change ($\Delta U^{o}$) is given by the equation:

$\Delta H^{o} = \Delta U^{o} + \Delta n_{g}RT$

where $\Delta n_{g}$ is the change in the number of moles of gaseous species in the reaction.

Calculating $\Delta n_{g}$:

$\Delta n_{g} = \sum n_{g, products} - \sum n_{g, reactants}$

$\Delta n_{g} = 7 - 11 = -4$

Substituting this value into the equation:

$\Delta H^{o} = \Delta U^{o} - 4RT$

Rearranging the terms to find the difference $\Delta H^{o} - \Delta U^{o}$:

$\Delta H^{o} - \Delta U^{o} = -4RT$

Alternatively, rearranging to find $\Delta U^{o} - \Delta H^{o}$:

$\Delta U^{o} - \Delta H^{o} = 4RT$

Answer: $\Delta U^o-\Delta H^o=4 R T$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A cone whose height is always equal to its diameter is increasing in volume at the rate of $40 \mathrm{~cm}^3 / \mathrm{sec}$. The rate at which the radius is increasing when its circular base is $1 \mathrm{~m}^2$ is
questions.solution:
Given the height $h$ of the cone is equal to its diameter $d = 2r$, so $h = 2r$.

The volume of the cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3} \pi r^2 h = \dfrac{1}{3} \pi r^2 (2r) = \dfrac{2}{3} \pi r^3$.

Differentiating with respect to time $t$, we get $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{2}{3} \pi (3r^2) \dfrac{dr}{dt} = 2 \pi r^2 \dfrac{dr}{dt}$.

Given $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 40 \text{ cm}^3/\text{sec}$. The area of the base is $A = \pi r^2 = 1 \text{ m}^2 = 10000 \text{ cm}^2$.

Substituting $A = \pi r^2 = 10000$ into the derivative equation: $40 = 2 \times (10000) \times \dfrac{dr}{dt}$.

Solving for $\dfrac{dr}{dt}$: $\dfrac{dr}{dt} = \dfrac{40}{20000} = \dfrac{4}{2000} = \dfrac{1}{500} = 0.002 \text{ cm/sec}$.

Answer: $0.002 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{sec}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The two equal sides of an isosceles triangle with a fixed base 'b' cm are decreasing at the rate of $4 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{sec}$. The rate at which the area is decreasing when each of the equal sides becomes equal to the base is
questions.solution:
Let the equal sides of the isosceles triangle be $x$ and the base be $b$. The height $h$ of the triangle is given by $h = \sqrt{x^2 - (b/2)^2} = \sqrt{x^2 - b^2/4}$.

The area $A$ of the triangle is $A = \dfrac{1}{2} \times b \times h = \dfrac{b}{2} \sqrt{x^2 - \dfrac{b^2}{4}}$.

Differentiating with respect to time $t$, we get $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{b}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x^2 - b^2/4}} \times 2x \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{bx}{2\sqrt{x^2 - b^2/4}} \dfrac{dx}{dt}$.

Given $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -4$ cm/sec and we need the rate of change when $x = b$.

Substituting $x = b$ into the expression for $\dfrac{dA}{dt}$:

$\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{b(b)}{2\sqrt{b^2 - b^2/4}} (-4) = \dfrac{b^2}{2\sqrt{3b^2/4}} (-4) = \dfrac{b^2}{2(b\sqrt{3}/2)} (-4) = \dfrac{b^2}{b\sqrt{3}} (-4) = -\dfrac{4b}{\sqrt{3}}$.

The area is decreasing at the rate of $\dfrac{4b}{\sqrt{3}}$ cm$^2$/sec.

Answer: $\dfrac{4 b}{\sqrt{3}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the area of region bounded by the lines $y=2 x+1, x$-axis, $x=a$ and $x=3$ is 10 sq units. Then the value of ' $a$ ' is
questions.solution:
The area $A$ of the region bounded by the line $y = 2x + 1$, the $x$-axis, $x = a$, and $x = 3$ is given by the definite integral of the function $f(x) = 2x + 1$ from $a$ to $3$.

$A = \int_{a}^{3} (2x + 1) dx = 10$

Evaluating the integral:

$[x^2 + x]_{a}^{3} = 10$

Substituting the limits:

$(3^2 + 3) - (a^2 + a) = 10$

$(9 + 3) - (a^2 + a) = 10$

$12 - a^2 - a = 10$

$a^2 + a - 2 = 0$

Factoring the quadratic equation:

$(a + 2)(a - 1) = 0$

The possible values for $a$ are $a = 1$ or $a = -2$. Since the region is bounded between $x = a$ and $x = 3$, and the line $y = 2x + 1$ intersects the $x$-axis at $x = -0.5$, we consider the positive value $a = 1$.

Answer: 1

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the curve $y^2=2 y-x$ and the $y$-axis is
questions.solution:
The given equation of the curve is $y^2 = 2y - x$, which can be rewritten as $x = 2y - y^2$.

The curve intersects the $y$-axis where $x = 0$. Setting $x = 0$ in the equation $x = 2y - y^2$, we get $2y - y^2 = 0$, which implies $y(2 - y) = 0$. Thus, the points of intersection are $y = 0$ and $y = 2$.

The area $A$ of the region bounded by the curve and the $y$-axis is given by the integral of $x$ with respect to $y$ from $y = 0$ to $y = 2$.

$A = \int_{0}^{2} (2y - y^2) dy$

Evaluating the integral:

$A = \left[ y^2 - \dfrac{y^3}{3} \right]_{0}^{2}$

$A = \left( 2^2 - \dfrac{2^3}{3} \right) - (0 - 0)$

$A = 4 - \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{12 - 8}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}$ sq units.

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{3}$ sq units

questions.q: The solution for the following system of inequalities $x+5 \leq 4(x-1) ; 3-2 x \gt -7$ on a real number line
questions.solution:

$x \lt 5$.

Combining the two results, we get $3 \leq x \lt 5$.
